narrative: Fire and climate stress dominate this week's ecology literature: post-fire shelters were shown to leave reptiles with shorter thermal activity windows, a Holocene charcoal and pollen record from Quebec found that topography shaped boreal fire regimes, and new sensor approaches now quantify wildlife exposure to wildfire smoke. Climate papers range from intensifying drought risk for global rainfed crops to the uncertain fate of Europe's mountain flora under warming. Movement and landscape work repeatedly points to connectivity, with step-selection predictions of corridors, newly planted woodlands increasing functional connectivity for several taxa, and mammals avoiding human presence rather than buildings during lockdowns. Population and trophic studies include an integrated territory-occupancy and mark-recapture model for spatial variation in survival and a mechanistic model of a compensatory ecological trap in seabirds. In invasion and community ecology, herbivorous crabs were found to aid an invasive salt-marsh grass, while island-area and isolation effects on interaction network roles and raptor coexistence via habitat segregation added to community theory. Methods contributions include a Python package for bioacoustic deep-learning models and an AI-driven extractor for counting microarthropods, alongside continuing debate over biodiversity indicators under land-use change.
